plan.why: The regain question is rising (BMJ meta-analysis, ScienceAlert Oct 18), and a habits framework is the kind of list people save. It's evergreen and well sourced, with an encouraging chronic-care tone. | fact-check: The framework is safe and evidence-based, but slide 4 misstates the BMJ meta-analysis (Weight regain after cessation of medication for weight management: systematic review and meta-analysis, BMJ, Jan 2026, PubMed 41500720). It covered 37 studies and more than 9,300 people. Average regain across all weight-management drugs was about 0.4 kg a month. About 0.8 kg a month applies to newer drugs (semaglutide and tirzepatide), with a projected return to baseline weight in about 1.5 years. Regain after stopping drugs was about 0.3 kg a month faster than after behavioural programmes ended (Oxford/NIHR BRC release, Science Media Centre). The '0.1 kg a month after behavioural programmes' figure wasn't confirmed, so verify it in the paper or replace it with the confirmed 'about 0.3 kg a month faster' comparison. Label the projections as modelled and the comparison as indirect (across studies). Also: carousels have reached 0–3 accounts on all 20 posts. The topic is good, but the owner should consider rebuilding it as a Short such as 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): what happens to weight after stopping?' (SURMOUNT-4).

package.title: Keeping GLP-1 Results Long Term: What 2 Big Studies Show

social.instagram_caption:
Worried the weight comes back after stopping a GLP-1? Here's what 2 big studies in adults with overweight or obesity show (group averages, not predictions), and why regain isn't a personal failing.

WHO calls obesity a chronic disease shaped by many complex factors. Studies show regain after stopping treatment is common, so long-term care plans matter.

• A 2026 BMJ review (37 studies, 9,300+ adults with overweight or obesity): average regain was 0.4 kg/month after stopping weight-management medicines overall. The semaglutide/tirzepatide subgroup, who also lost more while on treatment, averaged 0.8 kg/month (a subgroup average, not a head-to-head comparison), with a modelled return to starting weight around 1.5 years.

• SURMOUNT-4 (JAMA, 2024; adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes): people randomized to keep taking tirzepatide kept losing (−5.5% more, weeks 36–88), while those switched to placebo regained (+14.0%) over the same period. The most common side effects on tirzepatide were gut-related, like diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.

Bring these supportive habits with you — recommended, not proven on the drug itself: protein at meals (check first if you have kidney disease), strength training 2+ days/week (start gently), 150–300 min of moderate activity a week (WHO), fibre-rich foods, staying hydrated (unless told to limit fluids), and regular check-ins with your prescriber. They support a treatment plan but don't replace it.

factcheck.summary: The core numbers check out against primary sources. The BMJ 2026 meta-analysis (PMID 41500720, DOI 10.1136/bmj-2025-085304) reports 37 studies and 9,341 participants. Average regain was 0.4 kg/month. Regain was about 0.3 kg/month faster after stopping medication than after behavioural programmes ended. For semaglutide or tirzepatide, regain was 0.8 kg/month, with a modelled return to starting weight in about 1.5 years (confirmed via the Oxford press release). SURMOUNT-4 (JAMA 2024;331(1):38-48, online 11 Dec 2023) reports 783 enrolled, 670 randomised (335 vs 335), −20.9% during the lead-in, −5.5% vs +14.0% for weeks 36–88, −25.3% vs −9.9% overall, and 89.5% vs 16.6% keeping at least 80% of their loss. Its most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. The WHO obesity fact sheet (dated 7 Oct 2026) calls obesity a chronic disease. Safety caveats (kidney, fluids, start gently, don't stop or change medicines, disclaimer and prescriber line) are all there. There are six minor fixes: (1) the S4 WHO fact sheet doesn't print the 150–300 min or 2+ days figures, so cite the WHO 2020 guidelines instead; (2) the title promises 'what the evidence says helps', but the habits slide is honestly labelled 'not proven on the drug'; (3) the chart could read as 'newer drugs are worse' without the larger-initial-loss context; (4) 'treatment-related' isn't the source's term; (5) a missing timepoint on the ≥80% row; (6) the WHO wording on slide 2.
